In short: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has given a wide-ranging speech in an annual address. Ms von der Leyen suggested Canada could become the first "associate member" of the European Union, that Europe should build a new security council and that the world should slow down the pace of AI development. What's next? The 27 member states of the EU would have to decide whether to accept Canada as an associate member. abc.net.au/news/state-of-the-european-union-von-der-leyen-canada-associate-eu/107161710 Link copied Share Share article European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her bold vision for a strengthened, revitalised, united Europe and has invited a new name to the party: Canada. Ms von der Leyen covered a large range of topics in a 73-minute annual "state of the union" address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, leading off with the opening line from Charles Dickens's Tales of Two Cities, which she said also described the world today. "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times," she said. Here are five key takeaways from her speech. Oh, Canada! Ms von der Leyen said the European Union was opening the door for Canada to become its first associate member. "We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," she said. "So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU." Mark Carney received a standing ovation from the European Parliament. ( Reuters: Yves Herman ) Ms von der Leyen walked up to and embraced Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who she had invited to the address, and he received a standing ovation from the chamber. It will be up to the 27 EU member states whether Ms von der Leyen's proposal goes ahead. The US-Canada 'divorce' The US and Canada are often referred to as North American cousins, but the family feud has turned bitter as their trading relationship falls apart. The EU has historically resisted such types of flexible alliances that have no legal status. EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full membership. New security council The European Commission chief also pitched setting up a "European Security Council" with countries including Britain and Ukraine, as the continent grapples with the threat from Russia. "For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," Ms von der Leyen said. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. "This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality." Russia and Ukraine continue strikes on energy The US president declared both sides would refrain from striking energy-related targets as petrol and diesel prices rise. Europe is grappling with what it calls a campaign of "hybrid attacks" by Moscow aimed at undermining support for Ukraine, including recent attacks on Lithuania and Denmark and a Russian strike on the Ukraine–Poland border that just missed a train carrying diplomats, including former British prime minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt. "We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats," Ms von der Leyen said. "Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook. "We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents: Those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security." The European Commission president said she wanted to establish an "emergency security protocol" that would allow any EU member state to convene urgent talks in case of crisis. 'Strongest ever' support for Ukraine While the EU was struggling to counter Russian activities, Ms von der Leyen pledged that the bloc would ramp up support for Kyiv as Russia stepped up bombardments ahead of the winter. "We will give our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war," she said. "Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating." Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union. ( Reuters: Yves Herman ) Ms von der Leyen backed plans to jointly "develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system". She said that Europe would also step up its efforts to develop its own key military capabilities, pledging a "new European instrument for strategic enablers". Strengthened trade and manufacturing Ms von der Leyen said she would like Europe to build "an alliance for the future, to create a common prosperity" and economic security. "We will work on intelligent manufacturing," she said. "We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. "We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project." While Ursula von der Leyen was laying out her vision, animal rights activists demonstrated outside the European Parliament. ( Reuters: Yves Herman ) She said the EU would work on energy-critical minerals and batteries, on AI, quantum, cyber and economic security. "This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strengths," Ms von der Leyen said. Slow down on AI and social ban for kids Despite calling for more European technological advances, Ms von der Leyen said she supported the recent calls from tech leaders for a slowdown on AI. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon quit tech company Anthropic, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade". And earlier this week, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton and Anthropic's Dario Amodei both called for a global slowdown in AI development . "Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible," Ms von der Leyen said. Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is calling on the industry to slow down. "And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently from us." She pointed to recent incidents of rogue AI agents and warnings from developers . "CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models, to pace the frontier," Ms von der Leyen said. "If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too." Landmark EU rules governing the use of AI adopted recently put Europe in the position to shape global efforts to tackle the risks, Ms von der Leyen said. She said Europe would work with like-minded partners such as Canada, the United Kingdom and others to take measures such as model evaluation, verification and AI security. "I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier," von der Leyen said. She also proposed a social media ban for children under 13 — similar to Australia's world-first ban for kids under 16 — and no personal accounts for people under the age of 15, saying that platforms have to prove that they are safe for children. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-ukraine-agr.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OblT Oleshky has faced occupation from Russian forces since the invasion began in February 2022 Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement US first lady Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in the city of Oleshky , the White House announced Friday. The localized truce, according to the White House, is slated to begin on October 29. What do we know so far about the ceasefire deal in Oleshky? The Ukrainian city occupied by Russia on the frontline of the war faces a humanitarian crisis and only around 2,000 people still live there. Prior to the war, the city had a population of around 24,000. Oleshky has been under blockade since 2025 and was first occupied when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 . The city is located in southern Ukraine, just 9 kilometers (around 5.6 miles) from the major city of Kherson. "Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water," Melania Trump said in a statement. "The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks." Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, thanked the first lady for securing the deal. "Under our agreement: first a ceasefire will be put in place; second, humanitarian aid will be delivered to Oleshky; and third, civilians will be allowed to move freely out of Oleshky," Lubinets said in a video message posted on Telegram. "The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement." Russia also confirmed the agreement and said it will halt fire earlier than what the White House announced at 0400 local time (0100 GMT) on October 27. Oleshky faces constant attacks, with food and medicine scarce Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance According to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, residents in Oleshky say Russian occupying forces prevented them from leaving the city. Oleshky residents also say Russia has used civilians to shield military positions in the city — a war crime under international humanitarian law. Fresh Ukraine talks expected in Abu Dhabi next month The ceasefire deal in Oleshky comes as US, Ukrainian and Russian negotiators are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi next month to discuss ending the war. "The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskyy told the US conservative Hudson Institute think tank. US aims for new round of Russia-Ukraine negotiations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In comments to Russian state news outlet TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also said preparations are underway for a three-way meeting in mid-November. Russian President Vladimir Putin said security would be a main topic for the Abu Dhabi talks. "That is the security of both countries, Russia and Ukraine, after there has been a transition to a peace settlement," Peskov said. The Kremlin spokesperson said Russia only sees the Europeans at the table during a later stage in the talks. European leaders such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have said Europe must be involved in future Ukraine peace talks. "It is clear that the architecture of European security cannot be discussed without other participants," Peskov added. US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated at Zelenskyy, and is pressuring him to "make a deal." Trump has blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices in the US, as the US-Israeli war against Iran has caused the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and drove up the cost of gas at the pump for American consumers. Trump has backed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to lower prices at fuel pumps, drawing criticism from Ukraine . The Kremlin said Friday that the first tanker of Russian diesel has set sail for the US despite the backlash from Ukraine. Ukraine still dealing with Starshield issues as Trump defends Musk Most recently, there has been controversy that tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of the Starshield military communications system that Ukraine relies on, possibly with the backing of Trump. Trump has denied that he ordered restrictions on Starlink. He also defended Musk in comments to reporters on Friday and said, "Elon will never do anything wrong." "You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump said. "I guess the bottom line, he put it back ." Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Meanwhile, Zelenskyy and Ukraine said Friday that the system was still being throttled in Ukraine. "It works, but it's still limited," Zelenskyy told US broadcaster ABC News. A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told AFP news agency and other news outlets that Ukrainians were witnessing "instances of signal loss" when using Starshield. "There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted," the source added.
